questions.q: explain in your own words what had already happened at the Rhone.
points: Hannibal had already fought a battle against Scipio
Scipio was consul at the time
Hannibal had driven him back / defeated him

questions.lemma: cum hoc eodem … tertio idem Scipio
questions.q: how does Nepos emphasise that Hannibal kept beating the same Roman commander?
points: hoc eodem: ‘this same man’ stresses that it is the same commander again
idem Scipio repeats the point
tertio: Nepos counts the defeats
the historic presents decernit … dimittit make the second defeat vivid
sauciumque … ac fugatum: a humiliating picture of a consul both wounded and running
questions.guidance: Accept any three; each must refer to the Latin.

questions.q: how does Nepos make this victory sound swift and complete?
points: asyndeton: two short clauses with no connecting word
the battle is over as soon as it begins
utrosque: both consuls together are beaten
profligavit: a strong word, ‘crushed’
questions.guidance: Accept any two; each must refer to the Latin.

questions.q: what impression of Hannibal does Nepos create here, and how?
points: he seems human / vulnerable, a man who suffers
adeo gravi morbo: the illness is very severe
numquam: the harm to his eye is permanent
the suffering comes in the middle of his victories, which makes them more remarkable

questions.q: what happened to Flaminius?
points: he was a consul
at Lake Trasimene
he was surrounded / caught in an ambush
he was killed
together with his army

questions.q: what happened at this place?
points: (in 217 BC) Hannibal trapped Flaminius’ army
in mist between the hills and the lake shore
Flaminius was killed
with about 15,000 Romans

questions.q: who were these men?
points: the two consuls (of 216 BC) who commanded against Hannibal at Cannae

questions.q: what happened to Hannibal between the Rhone and his march into Etruria?
points: he fought Scipio at the Rhone and drove him back
he fought the same man again at Clastidium on the Po
Scipio was left wounded and routed
Scipio came against him a third time at the Trebia
with his colleague Tiberius Longus
Hannibal crushed them both
he crossed the Apennines through the land of the Ligurians
he caught a severe disease of the eyes
he never again had the full use of his right eye

questions.q: how does Nepos show the scale of Rome’s losses?
points: climax: the list rises from a consul to a group of ex-consuls
aliquot praeterea consulares: several former consuls died as well
Cn. Servilium Geminum: naming one victim makes the loss precise
qui superiore anno fuerat consul: he had been consul only a year before, which makes it personal for Roman readers
questions.guidance: Accept any three; each must refer to the Latin.

questions.q: explain in your own words what Hannibal did after the battle.
points: he marched on Rome
no one tried to stop him
he stayed for some time
in the hills close to the city

questions.lemma: in propinquis urbi montibus moratus est
questions.q: why might Roman readers find this detail alarming?
points: Hannibal was camped within sight of Rome
propinquis urbi stresses how close he was
moratus est (‘he lingered’) hints at a missed chance to attack
after nullo resistente, nothing stood between him and the city

questions.q: why was this city important to Hannibal at this time?
points: the richest city of Campania went over to him after Cannae
it served as his base

questions.q: how does Nepos make Hannibal’s escape seem impressive?
points: clausus: he appears trapped
locorum angustiis: the narrow ground leaves no way out
noctu: he gets a whole army out in the dark
sine ullo detrimento: ullo stresses that not a single man was lost
the superlative callidissimo praises the very man he fools
questions.guidance: Accept any three; each must refer to the Latin.

questions.lemma: quo repentino visu … nemo sit ausus
questions.q: how does Nepos emphasise the Romans’ fear?
points: repentino: the shock of the sudden sight
tantum terrorem: the size of the terror, with alliteration of t
the result clause ut … nemo sit ausus shows its effect
nemo: not one man dared
a whole Roman army stays behind its wall (extra vallum)
questions.guidance: Accept any three; each must refer to the Latin.

questions.q: explain how Hannibal defeated Minucius.
points: Minucius was Master of Horse
with power equal to the dictator’s
Hannibal lured him into battle
by a trick
and routed him

questions.q: what happened to Gracchus and Marcellus?
points: Gracchus was consul for the second time
he was lured into an ambush in Lucania
Hannibal destroyed him without being there himself
Marcellus had been consul five times
he was killed near Venusia
in the same way (by an ambush)

questions.q: who was Marcellus?
points: he captured Syracuse
he was called the Sword of Rome
he had been consul five times
he died in an ambush near Venusia (in 208 BC)

questions.q: how does Nepos emphasise Hannibal’s greatness?
points: hoc unum … satis: a single fact is enough to prove it
quantus ille fuerit: ille gives a grand, admiring tone
quamdiu in Italia fuit: the claim covers his whole time in Italy
anaphora of nemo … nemo drives the point home
post Cannensem pugnam: after Cannae no one even dared to camp near him
questions.guidance: Accept any three; each must refer to the Latin.

questions.q: describe how Hannibal outwitted Fabius and then Minucius.
points: he was trapped by the narrowness of the ground
he got his army out at night
without any loss
he tied bundles of twigs to the horns of young cattle
he set them alight
he sent many of the cattle scattering
the sudden sight terrified the Romans
no one dared to go outside the rampart
not many days later he lured Minucius (Master of Horse) into battle by a trick and routed him

questions.q: explain in your own words why Hannibal left Italy.
points: he was called home
to defend his own country
he left still unbeaten

questions.q: why do you think Nepos makes this the first word of the chapter?
points: it stresses that Hannibal left Italy unbeaten
so his record in Italy stands whatever happens at Zama
it secures the reader’s admiration before the defeat is told

questions.lemma: primo apud Rhodanum, iterum apud Padum, tertio apud Trebiam
questions.q: how does Nepos remind the reader of Hannibal’s earlier successes against this family?
points: tricolon of three battles
the numbered stages primo … iterum … tertio
repetition of apud with each place
the father’s defeats are recalled just as the son steps forward
questions.guidance: Accept any two; each must refer to the Latin.

questions.q: what impression of Hannibal’s motives does Nepos give, and how?
points: exhaustis … patriae facultatibus: Carthage’s weakness is given as the reason for seeking peace
so the blame for the defeat is moved away from Hannibal
impraesentiarum: the peace is only for the time being
quo valentior postea congrederetur: he is still planning the next war
even his peace offer is a military tactic

questions.q: why do you think Nepos describes the outcome of Zama so briefly?
points: the decisive defeat is told in a single word
Nepos moves quickly away from Hannibal’s only great loss
the focus shifts at once to the feat of the retreat
it keeps the reader’s admiration for Hannibal

questions.q: how does Nepos make the retreat seem remarkable?
points: incredibile dictu: Nepos himself steps in to marvel
biduo et duabus noctibus: the exact, very short time
circiter milia passuum trecenta: the huge distance
the precise numbers make the claim sound measured and real
the focus moves from defeat to a feat of endurance
questions.guidance: Accept any three; each must refer to the Latin.

questions.q: where was Hadrumetum?
points: a coastal city south of Carthage (modern Sousse in Tunisia)

questions.lemma: quos non solum effugit, sed etiam ipsos oppressit
questions.q: how does Nepos make Hannibal’s response to the ambush impressive?
points: non solum … sed etiam builds to a climax
escape alone would have been enough
oppressit: he crushes his attackers too
ipsos: the very men who ambushed him

questions.q: what happened to Hannibal at Zama and in the days that followed?
points: a few days after the meeting he fought Scipio at Zama
he was beaten
he reached Hadrumetum in two days and two nights
a distance of about three hundred miles
the Numidians who had left the battle with him ambushed him
he escaped them
and crushed them
at Hadrumetum he gathered the survivors
within a few days, by fresh recruiting, he assembled a large army

questions.q: what impression of Hannibal does this give, and how?
points: his energy / resilience after a crushing defeat
contrast of paucis (few days) and multos (many men)
the chapter ends on contraxit, an image of rebuilding

questions.q: how does Nepos show the split between Hannibal and his city?
points: contrast: Hannibal prepares for war while his city makes peace
acerrime: the superlative stresses his energy
the peace is made behind his back

questions.q: what does this phrase suggest about Hannibal’s attitude to the peace?
points: he carried on regardless
as if the peace did not apply to him
he stayed in command of the army

questions.q: who was Mago?
points: Hannibal’s younger brother
he fought with Hannibal in Italy
he later commanded in Spain and northern Italy

questions.q: how did the Carthaginian envoys try to win Rome’s goodwill?
points: they came to Rome to thank the senate and people
for making peace with them
they presented a golden crown
the thanks and the gift come before any request

questions.q: how does Nepos make the senate’s refusal stand out?
points: gratum acceptumque: the reply opens graciously
the first request is granted (obsides … futuros)
the balance makes the refusal captivos non remissuros sharp
indirect speech gives the cool, formal tone of an official decree
questions.guidance: Accept any three; each must refer to the Latin.

questions.q: explain in your own words why the senate would not return the prisoners.
points: the Carthaginians still kept Hannibal
in command of an army
he was the man responsible for starting the war
he was Rome’s bitterest enemy
his brother Mago was also still in command

questions.q: why is this word important in the senate’s reply?
points: Rome’s complaint is that Hannibal is still in command
it shows Roman suspicion that the war is not really over while he holds an army
it puts pressure on Carthage to remove him

questions.q: why might Roman readers be startled by this phrase, and what was the office really?
points: rex (‘king’) was a hated word at Rome
the office was that of suffete
one of Carthage’s two chief magistrates
elected for a single year

questions.q: what did the envoys say and ask at Rome, and how did the senate reply?
points: they thanked the Romans for making peace
they presented a golden crown
they asked that their hostages be kept at Fregellae
they asked for their prisoners back
the senate said the gift was welcome and accepted
the hostages could stay where they asked
the prisoners would not be returned
because Hannibal was still in command of an army
and so was his brother Mago

questions.q: how does Nepos help his Roman readers understand Carthage’s government?
points: he compares the office with the Roman consulship
the balanced ut … sic sets the two cities side by side
annui bini: two each year, just like the consuls
Carthage is made to look like a mirror of Rome

essays.q: how does Nepos present the Roman commanders who face Hannibal?
points: Scipio fights Hannibal again and again and is beaten each time
Scipio is left wounded and in flight, a humiliating image for a consul
even two consuls together at the Trebia are crushed
Flaminius falls into an ambush and dies with his army
Centenius and Rome’s picked troops are destroyed
Rome sends both consuls at once against Hannibal at Cannae, a sign of desperation
Paulus and several ex-consuls are killed, so a whole layer of Rome’s leadership is lost

essays.q: how does Nepos make Hannibal seem both human and unstoppable?
points: he presses on over the Apennines towards Etruria
he is struck by a severe eye disease
he never again has the full use of his right eye
still ill and carried in a litter, he ambushes and kills the consul Flaminius and his army
soon after he destroys Centenius and his picked troops
in Apulia he routs the armies of both consuls in a single battle
he kills the consul Paulus and several ex-consuls

essays.lemma: hac pugna pugnata … nemo sit ausus
essays.q: how does Nepos make Hannibal’s dealings with Fabius dramatic?
points: after Cannae Hannibal marches on Rome unopposed and camps in the hills near the city
Fabius, the dictator, is given his full name and title as a serious opponent
Hannibal appears trapped in narrow ground
he escapes at night without losing a man
Fabius, the most cunning of commanders, is himself deceived
the strange night-time trick with burning twigs on the horns of cattle
the sudden sight terrifies the Romans so that no one leaves the rampart

essays.q: how does Nepos convince the reader of Hannibal’s greatness as a general?
points: he lures Minucius into battle by a trick, though Minucius has power equal to the dictator’s
he destroys Gracchus, twice consul, by an ambush without being present
he kills Marcellus, five times consul, in the same way
his victims grow steadily more senior
Nepos says it would take too long to list every battle
one fact is said to be enough to prove his greatness
no one stood against him in battle in Italy, and after Cannae no one camped against him

essays.q: how does Nepos make this passage fast-moving and vivid?
points: the story moves from Italy to Africa in a single sentence
the peace talks are dismissed in two short clauses
the defeat at Zama is told in one word
the retreat is astonishingly fast, with exact times and distances
his own companions in flight suddenly ambush him
he escapes and crushes them
within a few days he has a large army again

essays.lemma: post id factum … C. Aurelium consules
essays.q: how does Nepos present Hannibal’s energy and determination?
points: after his defeat at Zama he covers about three hundred miles in two days and two nights
he beats off and crushes the Numidians who ambush him
he gathers the survivors at Hadrumetum
he raises a large new army within a few days
he throws himself into preparations for more war
Carthage makes peace while he is still preparing
he nonetheless stays in command and carries on operations in Africa, with his brother Mago

essays.q: how does Nepos present the Romans’ attitude towards Hannibal?
points: the senate accepts Carthage’s gift graciously
it grants the request about the hostages
it refuses to return the prisoners while Hannibal commands an army
it blames Hannibal personally for starting the war
it calls him the bitterest enemy of the Roman name
it is suspicious that he still holds a command, along with Mago
its reply alone is enough to make Carthage recall him

essays.q: how does Nepos show Carthage’s weakness in its dealings with Rome after the war?
points: Carthaginian envoys come to Rome to thank the Romans for making peace
they present a golden crown
they ask favours humbly, about their hostages and prisoners
the senate grants one request and refuses the other
the refusal is based on Carthage’s own general
Carthage obeys at once and recalls Hannibal and Mago
even Carthage’s highest office is explained by comparison with Rome’s
